distractors.D: Right-to-audit is a later contract clause for ongoing oversight, not pre-selection research.

explanation.exam_pattern: Vendor SELECTION = due diligence + watch for conflicts of interest. Supply-chain analysis is part of due diligence.

questions.stem: A security team already works with a critical SaaS vendor and wants to establish ONGOING third-party risk MONITORING (as opposed to one-time onboarding checks). Which TWO of the following are forms of ongoing monitoring? (Choose two.)

options.text: Performing the initial financial and background due-diligence check before signing
Sending the vendor periodic security questionnaires
Negotiating the master service agreement terms
Reviewing the vendor's recurring independent audit reports (e.g., annual SOC 2 Type II)

explanation.correct: Ongoing monitoring tracks a vendor's posture over time — periodic questionnaires and reviewing their recurring independent audit/attestation reports are classic examples.

distractors.A: Initial due diligence happens once, during SELECTION/onboarding — it is not ongoing monitoring.
distractors.C: Negotiating the MSA is a one-time onboarding/contracting activity, not continuous monitoring.

explanation.exam_pattern: Separate the vendor lifecycle: selection (due diligence) -> contracting (MSA/SLA) -> ONGOING monitoring (questionnaires, recurring independent assessments, right-to-audit).

questions.stem: Under GDPR, an online retailer decides what customer personal data to collect and why, then contracts a cloud email service to send marketing messages strictly on the retailer's instructions. What is the cloud email service's role?

explanation.correct: A processor handles personal data on behalf of, and under the instructions of, the controller. The cloud email service only acts as the retailer directs — it is the processor.

distractors.A: 'Data owner' is an internal accountability role, not the GDPR controller/processor distinction asked here.
distractors.B: The controller determines the PURPOSES and MEANS of processing — that is the retailer, not the service.
distractors.C: A data subject is the individual the personal data is about (the customers).

explanation.exam_pattern: Controller decides why/how (purposes & means); processor acts on the controller's instructions. The one who decides is the controller.

questions.stem: A customer submits a formal request under GDPR demanding that a company erase all personal data it holds about them. Which data-subject right is being exercised?

options.text: Right to be forgotten (right to erasure)

explanation.correct: The right to be forgotten (erasure) lets a data subject require deletion of their personal data when there is no overriding reason to keep it.

distractors.A: Rectification is the right to correct inaccurate data, not to erase it.
distractors.B: Data minimization is a principle (collect only what is needed), not a deletion request a subject files.
distractors.C: Data portability is the right to receive one's data in a usable format and move it elsewhere, not to delete it.

explanation.exam_pattern: GDPR data-subject rights: erasure (be forgotten) = delete, portability = move, rectification = correct, access = see.

questions.stem: A healthcare provider is found to have violated HIPAA, and regulators impose a $1.5 million monetary penalty. Which consequence of non-compliance is this?

explanation.correct: A monetary penalty imposed by a regulator for breaking a law/regulation is a fine — a direct financial consequence of non-compliance.

distractors.A: Contractual penalties arise from breaching an agreement between parties, not a regulator's fine.
distractors.C: Loss of license is revocation of the ability to operate, not a fine.
distractors.D: Reputational damage is lost trust/brand harm, which is indirect and not a monetary penalty.

explanation.exam_pattern: Non-compliance consequences: fines/sanctions (regulatory $), reputational damage, loss of license, contractual impacts. Match the SOURCE of the penalty.

questions.stem: To demonstrate compliance, every employee must read the updated security policy and digitally sign a statement confirming they have read, understood, and agree to follow it. This compliance-monitoring practice is BEST called:

explanation.correct: Having users formally confirm (sign) that they have read and accept a policy is attestation/acknowledgement — a common internal compliance-monitoring method.

distractors.B: Due diligence is investigative homework (e.g., before a vendor engagement), not a signed acknowledgement.
distractors.C: A data inventory catalogs what data the organization holds; it is unrelated to policy sign-off.
distractors.D: An external audit is an independent outside party examining controls, not users signing a policy.

explanation.exam_pattern: Compliance monitoring includes attestation/acknowledgement, internal vs external review, due care/diligence, and automation. Signed policy = attestation.

questions.stem: An organization's own security staff periodically examine its controls for policy compliance and report the findings to the board's audit committee. This is BEST described as:

explanation.correct: Work performed by the organization's OWN staff and reported to its audit committee is an internal audit (internal compliance review / self-assessment).

distractors.A: An independent third-party assessment is performed by an outside firm for objectivity.
distractors.B: A regulatory examination is conducted by an outside regulator (external), not internal staff.
distractors.D: A penetration test actively attacks systems to find exploitable weaknesses — a different activity.

explanation.exam_pattern: Internal (own staff, audit committee, self-assessment) vs external (regulators, examinations, independent third-party). Who performs it decides the category.

questions.stem: Early in an authorized penetration test, the tester collects information about the target only from publicly available sources — WHOIS records, the company website, job postings, and social media — without sending any packets to the target's systems. This phase is:

explanation.correct: Passive reconnaissance gathers intelligence from third-party/public sources without directly interacting with the target, so it leaves no trace on the target's systems.

distractors.A: Vulnerability scanning actively probes systems for weaknesses — it is an active technique.
distractors.B: Lateral movement is pivoting between systems AFTER an initial compromise, not information gathering.
distractors.C: Active reconnaissance DOES touch the target (pings, port scans, banner grabbing) and can be detected.

explanation.exam_pattern: Passive recon = no contact with target (OSINT). Active recon = direct interaction (scans/probes), potentially detectable.

questions.stem: A client provides a penetration-testing team with LIMITED information — standard user credentials and a partial network diagram — but withholds full architecture and source-code details. Which testing environment is this?

explanation.correct: Partial information up front = partially known (gray-box) testing, balancing realism with efficiency by giving the tester a limited foothold of knowledge.

distractors.A: A credentialed scan is automated scanning using valid logins, not an adversarial pen-test engagement.
distractors.B: Known (white-box) provides FULL information (architecture, source, configs) up front.
distractors.C: Unknown (black-box) gives the tester NO prior information — they must discover everything.

explanation.exam_pattern: Pen-test knowledge levels: known = white-box (full), partially known = gray-box (some), unknown = black-box (none).

questions.stem: An organization runs an exercise in which the offensive team and the defensive team collaborate and share information in real time to improve detection and response together. Which type of engagement is this?

explanation.correct: Integrated testing (purple team) has the attackers and defenders work TOGETHER, sharing findings live so defenses improve faster than either side acting alone.

distractors.B: Unknown-environment refers to how much INFORMATION the tester has, not to red/blue/purple collaboration.
distractors.C: A blue team (defensive) defends and responds; on its own it is not the combined exercise described.
distractors.D: A red team (offensive) attacks independently to emulate an adversary, without collaborating with defenders.

explanation.exam_pattern: Offensive = red, defensive = blue, integrated = purple (red + blue collaborating).

questions.stem: Security-awareness training teaches employees to notice and report a coworker who suddenly begins accessing and downloading large volumes of sensitive files unrelated to their role, often outside business hours. Recognizing this is BEST categorized under which awareness topic?

explanation.correct: Unusual, out-of-pattern activity like bulk access to unrelated sensitive data is anomalous behavior that may signal an insider threat — a core recognition goal of awareness programs.

distractors.B: Phishing recognition is about spotting malicious emails/messages, not a coworker's data-access pattern.
distractors.C: Password management covers strong, unique credentials and managers — unrelated to spotting insider activity.
distractors.D: Secure remote-work guidance covers VPN/device practices, not recognizing anomalous insider behavior.

explanation.exam_pattern: Anomalous-behavior recognition (risky/unexpected/unintentional) trains users to spot and report insider-threat indicators.

questions.stem: A training module instructs staff not to discuss unreleased project details in public, not to post photos of their access badges or screens on social media, and to consider what small pieces of information an adversary could aggregate. Which awareness topic does this cover?

explanation.correct: OPSEC teaches users to protect seemingly harmless information that an adversary could piece together to harm the organization — exactly the badge/social-media/project-detail guidance.

distractors.A: Change management governs approving IT changes, unrelated to information-leakage awareness.
distractors.B: Password management is about credential hygiene, not controlling incidental information disclosure.
distractors.C: Secure media disposal covers destroying data on retired drives/paper, not social-media/OPSEC leakage.

explanation.exam_pattern: OPSEC = protect small, aggregable pieces of information adversaries could combine. A common user-training topic alongside social engineering and insider threat.

questions.stem: Employees are trained to stay alert to their physical surroundings — challenging unfamiliar people who lack a visible badge and never holding a secured door open for someone they do not recognize. Which user-training topic does this reinforce?

explanation.correct: Being alert to one's surroundings and the people in them — and refusing to enable tailgating — is situational awareness applied to physical security.

distractors.A: Phishing recognition targets malicious messages, not in-person tailgating.
distractors.B: Password management concerns credential hygiene, not physical alertness.
distractors.C: Change-management procedure governs IT change approval, not physical vigilance.

explanation.exam_pattern: Situational awareness trains users to notice and respond to their physical environment (e.g., stopping tailgating/piggybacking at secure doors).

questions.stem: An organization is building the hybrid/remote-work section of its security-awareness program. Which TWO practices SHOULD this module teach employees? (Choose two.)

options.text: Share your VPN credentials with a teammate who forgot theirs
Connect through the company VPN when using untrusted or public Wi-Fi
Lock the screen when away and keep household members off work devices
Disable disk encryption on the laptop to improve performance

explanation.correct: Remote-work guidance should promote VPN use on untrusted networks and basic device discipline (screen locking, keeping work devices restricted to the employee) to protect data off-site.

distractors.A: Sharing VPN credentials breaks accountability and authentication and must never be taught as acceptable.
distractors.D: Disabling disk encryption removes protection for data at rest if the device is lost or stolen — the opposite of secure practice.

explanation.exam_pattern: Hybrid/remote-work awareness: VPN on untrusted networks, device locking, home-network hygiene. Reject anything that weakens encryption or shares credentials.

questions.stem: An administrator must apply one hardened configuration (password policy, disabled services, audit settings) to hundreds of domain-joined Windows workstations AND have it automatically reapplied if a user changes a setting. Which tool is BEST?

options.text: A one-time manual checklist run on each PC

explanation.correct: Group Policy centrally defines and continuously ENFORCES the baseline across every domain-joined host, reapplying settings on refresh — the configuration enforcement the objective calls for.

distractors.B: A host firewall controls network traffic to/from the host, not the full set of OS configuration settings.
distractors.C: A manual checklist does not scale to hundreds of hosts and does not reapply the setting if a user changes it.
distractors.D: Full-disk encryption protects data at rest; it does not enforce a configuration baseline.

explanation.exam_pattern: Consistent, self-healing config across many hosts = baseline/config enforcement via Group Policy (Windows) or similar config-management tooling.

questions.stem: Laptops issued to a travelling sales team are frequently lost. Which hardening control MOST directly protects the confidentiality of data on a stolen laptop's drive, even if the thief removes the drive?

explanation.correct: FDE encrypts the entire volume, so data is unreadable without the key even if the drive is pulled and attached to another machine.

distractors.A: Disabling USB ports reduces peripheral attack surface but does not protect data stored on the disk.
distractors.B: A screensaver password is bypassed by removing the drive and reading it elsewhere.
distractors.D: A HIDS detects suspicious activity on a running system; it does nothing for a powered-off drive removed by a thief.

explanation.exam_pattern: Lost/stolen device + protect data AT REST = full-disk encryption (often with a TPM).

questions.stem: A plant runs legacy ICS/SCADA controllers that cannot be patched or run an EDR agent without voiding vendor support. Which hardening approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Expose them directly to the internet so the vendor can patch remotely
Install consumer desktop antivirus on each controller
Place them on an isolated, segmented network with strict access controls

explanation.correct: When specialized/embedded systems can't be patched or protected directly, isolating and segmenting them behind tight access controls is the standard compensating hardening measure.

distractors.A: Exposing fragile OT controllers to the internet dramatically increases risk — the opposite of hardening.
distractors.B: These controllers often cannot run standard AV, and doing so is typically unsupported and can destabilize them.
distractors.C: Automatic updates can break fragile ICS/SCADA and are usually unsupported on such systems.

explanation.exam_pattern: Unpatchable ICS/SCADA/embedded/RTOS → isolate + segment + restrict access (compensating control).

questions.stem: Before deploying new IoT cameras and network switches, the FIRST item on the hardening checklist is to change the vendor-supplied admin credentials. Why is this so important?

options.text: Changing them automatically enables full-disk encryption
Default credentials are publicly documented and heavily targeted by attackers
It is required before any host firewall port can open
Default passwords use weak hashing that slows the device down

explanation.correct: Vendor default usernames/passwords are listed in manuals and online databases and are among the first things attackers and botnets (e.g., Mirai) try.

distractors.A: Credentials are unrelated to enabling disk encryption.
distractors.C: Changing a password has nothing to do with opening firewall ports.
distractors.D: The risk is public knowledge of the credential, not hashing performance.

explanation.exam_pattern: Hardening always includes removing/changing DEFAULT accounts and passwords.

questions.stem: A hospital must dispose of FAILED SSDs that held patient records. The drives are dead (cannot be overwritten) and degaussing does not work on them. Which method ensures the data cannot be recovered?

options.text: Sending the drives to the recycle bin and emptying it

explanation.correct: Flash/SSD media have no magnetic domains and the drives are unwriteable, so physical destruction is the reliable sanitization method here.

distractors.B: Emptying the recycle bin removes pointers, not the data itself.
distractors.C: A format leaves the underlying data recoverable, and a dead drive may not format at all.
distractors.D: Degaussing only affects magnetic media (HDD/tape); it has no effect on solid-state flash.

explanation.exam_pattern: Dead or flash media that can't be overwritten/degaussed → destroy (shred/pulverize/incinerate).

questions.stem: An organization pays a third-party vendor to destroy decommissioned drives off-site. What should it obtain for each batch to prove destruction occurred for audit and compliance purposes?

options.text: Only a verbal confirmation from the driver

explanation.correct: A certificate of destruction documents what was destroyed, when, how, and by whom — the evidence auditors expect for sanitized/decommissioned assets.

distractors.A: A verbal confirmation is not auditable evidence.
distractors.B: A license key is unrelated to media disposal.
distractors.D: A pentest report assesses exploitable weaknesses, not disposal.

explanation.exam_pattern: Third-party disposal/decommissioning → require a certificate of destruction (certification).

questions.stem: A company is sanitizing HDDs that will be REUSED internally (not destroyed). Which TWO methods sanitize the data while keeping the drives usable? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Cryptographic erase (destroying the encryption keys on a self-encrypting drive)
Deleting the files and emptying the recycle bin
Overwriting/wiping the drive with a multi-pass pattern

explanation.correct: Overwriting (NIST 'clear') and cryptographic erase (destroying the keys) both render the old data unrecoverable while leaving the drive functional for reuse.

distractors.B: Degaussing erases a magnetic HDD's factory servo tracks, destroying the drive — it cannot be reused.
distractors.C: Deleting files and emptying the bin leaves the data fully recoverable — it is not sanitization.
distractors.D: Shredding physically destroys the drive; reuse is impossible.

explanation.exam_pattern: Reuse → overwrite or crypto-erase. Dispose for good → degauss (HDD) or destroy (shred).

questions.stem: A scan returns three findings with CVSS base scores of 9.8, 5.4, and 2.1. With limited time and all else equal, which should the team remediate FIRST?

explanation.correct: CVSS base scores rank severity (9.0–10.0 = Critical). Prioritizing the 9.8 addresses the greatest risk first.

distractors.A: A 2.1 Low poses the least risk of the three.
distractors.C: A 5.4 Medium is lower severity than a 9.8 Critical.
distractors.D: Discovery order is not a measure of risk; severity (and exploitability/exposure) is.

explanation.exam_pattern: CVSS: 0.1–3.9 Low, 4.0–6.9 Medium, 7.0–8.9 High, 9.0–10.0 Critical — remediate highest risk first.

questions.stem: A scanner flags a server as vulnerable to a CVE based on its version string, but manual verification shows the vendor backported the fix and the server is NOT actually vulnerable. How should this result be classified?

explanation.correct: The tool reported a vulnerability that does not actually exist — a false positive, a common result of version-only checks against backported patches.

distractors.A: A true positive is a correctly reported, genuinely present vulnerability.
distractors.B: A false negative is a real vulnerability the scanner MISSED, not a phantom one it reported.
distractors.C: A zero-day is an unknown/unpatched flaw; here the issue is already fixed.

explanation.exam_pattern: Reported-but-not-real = false positive; real-but-missed = false negative. Always validate before remediating.

questions.stem: A security engineer analyzes an application's SOURCE CODE for flaws BEFORE it is compiled or executed, without running it. Which technique is this?

explanation.correct: SAST (static analysis) inspects source/bytecode without executing the program, catching issues early in development.

distractors.B: A network scan probes hosts/services, not application source code.
distractors.C: Fuzzing feeds malformed input to a RUNNING app — it requires execution.
distractors.D: DAST tests the running application from the outside, without source code.

explanation.exam_pattern: Static = analyze code at rest (SAST); Dynamic = test the app while it runs (DAST/fuzzing).

questions.stem: A critical vulnerability has been confirmed and patched on all affected servers. Which TWO actions CLOSE OUT the finding in a mature vulnerability-management process? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Update reporting and metrics to reflect the remediation
Reclassify the finding as a zero-day
Permanently disable all future vulnerability scanning
Delete the affected servers from the asset inventory
Rescan/validate the hosts to confirm the vulnerability is remediated

explanation.correct: Validation by rescanning confirms the fix actually worked, and updating reporting/metrics documents closure for stakeholders and audits.

distractors.B: A patched flaw is not a zero-day; reclassifying it is simply incorrect.
distractors.C: Disabling scanning removes the visibility needed to catch new and recurring issues.
distractors.D: Assets stay in inventory after patching; removing them would hide them from future scans.

explanation.exam_pattern: Response lifecycle closeout = validation (rescan) + reporting. Never 'fix and forget.'

questions.stem: A company wants to automatically detect and BLOCK outbound emails that contain credit-card or Social Security numbers. Which tool is purpose-built for this?

explanation.correct: DLP inspects content against patterns/classifications and can block or quarantine data (like PII/PAN) before it leaves the organization.

distractors.A: NetFlow records flow metadata (who/where/how much), not message content.
distractors.C: A SIEM aggregates and correlates logs to alert; it is not an inline content-blocking control.
distractors.D: SNMP traps report device status/events, not sensitive-data egress.

explanation.exam_pattern: Inspect content + stop sensitive data leaving = DLP (endpoint, network, and cloud/email).

questions.stem: An analyst needs to see which internal hosts talked to an external IP, over which ports, and how much data moved — WITHOUT capturing full packet payloads. Which data source is BEST?

options.text: Full packet capture of every byte

explanation.correct: NetFlow summarizes conversations (source/destination, ports, byte/packet counts) — exactly the metadata asked for, without storing payloads.

distractors.B: AV quarantine logs only record malware the AV handled, not general traffic flows.
distractors.C: Full packet capture includes payloads — more than requested, with far higher storage cost.
distractors.D: A vault log tracks credential checkouts, not network conversations.

explanation.exam_pattern: Flow metadata (talkers/ports/volume) without payload = NetFlow/IPFIX; full content = packet capture.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants a standardized, automated way for different security tools to exchange configuration-compliance and vulnerability data — for example, checking hosts against a CIS benchmark. Which standard provides this interoperability?

explanation.correct: SCAP is a suite of specifications (CVE, CVSS, OVAL, XCCDF, CPE) that lets tools share and automate compliance and vulnerability content consistently, e.g., evaluating CIS/DISA benchmarks.

distractors.A: SMTP is the email transport protocol.
distractors.B: NetFlow describes traffic flows, not configuration compliance content.
distractors.D: SNMP monitors and manages device state; it is not a security-content exchange standard.

explanation.exam_pattern: Automated, tool-agnostic compliance/benchmark checking = SCAP (with its component specs).

questions.stem: A SOC needs deep, continuous telemetry from laptops that frequently work remotely, off the corporate VPN. Which monitoring approach is MOST suitable?

options.text: Manual log review performed once a quarter
Agent-based monitoring with software installed on each endpoint
Agentless monitoring that only polls devices reachable on the LAN
Disabling endpoint logging to conserve bandwidth

explanation.correct: An installed agent collects rich data locally and forwards it whenever the host has connectivity, so remote/off-LAN laptops are still covered.

distractors.A: Quarterly manual review cannot provide continuous, near-real-time monitoring.
distractors.C: Agentless polling needs the device to be reachable over the network and gives shallower data — it fails for off-LAN laptops.
distractors.D: Disabling logging eliminates the visibility the SOC needs.

explanation.exam_pattern: Remote/deep/continuous telemetry → agent-based. Lightweight, no-install, on-net checks → agentless.

questions.stem: A user signs in to a third-party web application with their corporate identity; the identity provider sends an XML-based assertion to the app to establish the authenticated web-SSO session. Which protocol is in use?

explanation.correct: SAML exchanges XML-based assertions between an IdP and a service provider to federate authentication for web SSO — exactly the flow described.

distractors.B: LDAP is a directory-access protocol for querying an identity store, not a federation assertion.
distractors.C: OAuth 2.0 is an AUTHORIZATION framework that delegates access via tokens; it is not an XML authentication assertion.
distractors.D: OIDC adds authentication on top of OAuth but uses JSON Web Tokens, not XML/SAML assertions.

explanation.exam_pattern: XML assertion for web SSO = SAML. Token-based delegated authZ = OAuth. Identity layer on OAuth (JWT) = OIDC.

questions.stem: In a system, access is decided by security LABELS (e.g., Confidential, Secret, Top Secret) assigned and enforced by the operating system, and users CANNOT change permissions on objects they own. Which access-control model is this?

explanation.correct: MAC enforces access via system-assigned classification labels and clearances; owners cannot override them — common in government/military and SELinux.

distractors.A: RBAC grants access based on job role, not classification labels.
distractors.B: DAC lets the data OWNER grant/change permissions at their discretion — the opposite of this scenario.
distractors.D: ABAC makes dynamic decisions from attributes/policies (department, time, location), not fixed labels.

explanation.exam_pattern: System-enforced labels/clearances, owner can't override = MAC. Owner-controlled = DAC.

questions.stem: A company wants administrators to receive elevated rights ONLY for the short window they need them, with the credential checked out from a vault and automatically expired afterward. Which capability provides this?

options.text: A shared admin password stored in a team wiki
Self-service password reset for standard users
Just-in-time (JIT) privileged access through a PAM solution
Permanent membership in the Domain Admins group

explanation.correct: A PAM platform grants just-in-time, time-boxed elevation with password vaulting and ephemeral credentials, minimizing standing privilege.

distractors.A: A shared static password is untracked and insecure, defeating accountability.
distractors.B: Self-service reset helps normal users recover passwords; it is not privilege elevation.
distractors.D: Permanent admin membership is standing privilege — the very thing JIT avoids.

explanation.exam_pattern: Temporary, vaulted, auto-expiring elevated access = PAM with JIT and ephemeral credentials.

questions.stem: Which TWO of the following are examples of the 'something you HAVE' authentication factor? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A one-time code generated by a TOTP authenticator app on a phone

explanation.correct: A physical security key and a phone generating a TOTP code are both possession factors — 'something you have.'

distractors.A: A memorized PIN is a knowledge factor — 'something you KNOW.'
distractors.C: A fingerprint is a biometric — 'something you ARE.'
distractors.D: Keystroke/typing rhythm is a behavioral factor — 'something you DO.'

explanation.exam_pattern: Factors: know (password/PIN), have (token/phone/key), are (biometric), do (behavior), where (location).

questions.stem: When a specific IOC is detected, a SOC wants to automatically enrich the alert, open a ticket, and isolate the host by following a predefined, repeatable workflow. Which technology and artifact enable this?

options.text: A shared spreadsheet of manual steps
A SIEM dashboard with no automated actions

explanation.correct: SOAR orchestrates tools and runs playbooks to execute a defined response sequence automatically and consistently.

distractors.A: A manual spreadsheet is neither automated nor consistently repeatable at machine speed.
distractors.B: A scanner finds vulnerabilities; it does not orchestrate incident response.
distractors.C: A SIEM alone correlates and alerts, but it does not orchestrate multi-tool response actions.

explanation.exam_pattern: Automated, repeatable, multi-step response = SOAR + playbooks/runbooks (often API integrations).

questions.stem: Before automating its entire provisioning pipeline, a team realizes that one flaw in the central automation script could simultaneously misconfigure EVERY new system it builds. Which consideration of automation does this illustrate?

explanation.correct: Centralizing logic means a single defect can propagate everywhere at once — the automation becomes a single point of failure, a key risk/consideration.

distractors.A: Faster reaction time is a BENEFIT of automation, not the risk described.
distractors.B: Consistent baseline enforcement is a benefit, not the concentrated-risk problem here.
distractors.C: Scalability is a benefit of automation, not the downside illustrated.

explanation.exam_pattern: Automation considerations/risks: complexity, cost, technical debt, and single point of failure.

questions.stem: A team uses automation to apply the exact same hardened configuration to every server it provisions, eliminating manual configuration drift. Which BENEFIT of automation does this BEST demonstrate?

options.text: Slowing down the team's reaction time
Enforcing secure baselines consistently and at scale
Creating a single point of failure

explanation.correct: Automation applies the same baseline identically to every host, enforcing consistency and removing human error/drift — a core benefit.

distractors.A: Technical debt is a drawback/consideration, not the benefit shown.
distractors.B: Automation speeds reaction time; it does not slow it.
distractors.D: A single point of failure is a risk of automation, not this benefit.

explanation.exam_pattern: Benefits: efficiency, scale, consistent baseline enforcement, and faster reaction time.

questions.stem: After an incident is fully resolved, the team meets to document what happened, what worked, and what to improve, feeding the findings back into their plans. Which incident-response phase is this?

explanation.correct: The post-incident lessons-learned review captures improvements and feeds them back into preparation — the final phase of the IR lifecycle.

distractors.A: Detection identifies that an incident is occurring.
distractors.C: Eradication removes the threat from affected systems.
distractors.D: Containment limits the spread/damage of an active incident.

explanation.exam_pattern: IR order: Preparation → Detection/Analysis → Containment → Eradication → Recovery → Lessons Learned.

questions.stem: An organization gathers stakeholders in a conference room to TALK THROUGH their response to a hypothetical ransomware scenario — no production systems are touched. Which type of exercise is this?

explanation.correct: A tabletop is a discussion-based walkthrough of the plan against a scenario, with no systems actually affected — ideal for validating roles and decisions cheaply.

distractors.A: A failover test actually switches operations to backup systems.
distractors.B: A penetration test actively attacks systems to find exploitable weaknesses.
distractors.D: A simulation actually executes/mimics the attack and response on systems, not just discussion.

explanation.exam_pattern: Discussion-based = tabletop; hands-on execution against systems = simulation.

questions.stem: Instead of waiting for alerts, analysts form a hypothesis (e.g., 'an attacker may be abusing living-off-the-land binaries') and proactively search historical data for signs of a compromise that evaded existing detections. What is this activity called?

explanation.correct: Threat hunting is proactive, hypothesis-driven searching for adversary activity that automated alerting missed.

distractors.B: A legal hold preserves data for litigation — unrelated to proactive searching.
distractors.C: Containment limits damage from an already-detected incident.
distractors.D: Root cause analysis determines WHY a known incident happened, after it is identified.

explanation.exam_pattern: Proactive, hypothesis-based search for undetected threats = threat hunting (not alert-driven).

questions.stem: To keep digital evidence admissible, investigators document every person who handled it, when, and why, from collection through presentation in court. Which concept does this documentation establish?

explanation.correct: Chain of custody is the unbroken, documented record of who controlled the evidence at every step, proving it was not altered.

distractors.B: E-discovery is identifying and producing electronically stored information for litigation.
distractors.C: Order of volatility governs the SEQUENCE of collection (RAM before disk), not handling records.
distractors.D: A legal hold preserves data from deletion; it does not track handling.

explanation.exam_pattern: Documented who/when/why handling of evidence for admissibility = chain of custody.

questions.stem: Before analysis, a forensic examiner connects a suspect drive through a write blocker, creates a bit-for-bit image, and records a hash of BOTH the original and the copy. Why hash both?

options.text: To speed up the imaging process
To encrypt the evidence so it stays confidential
To compress the image and save storage space
To prove the image is an exact, unaltered copy and to detect any later tampering

explanation.correct: Matching hashes of the source and the image prove the copy is identical (preservation/integrity); re-hashing later detects any change. The write blocker ensures the original is never modified.

distractors.A: Hashing verifies integrity; it does not speed up acquisition.
distractors.B: Hashing provides integrity, not confidentiality — it does not encrypt.
distractors.C: A hash is a fixed-length digest; it does not compress the data.

explanation.exam_pattern: Forensic acquisition = write blocker + bit-for-bit image + matching hashes (integrity/preservation).

questions.stem: Anticipating litigation, a company issues a formal directive requiring staff and IT to preserve all relevant emails and documents and to suspend routine deletion. What is this directive called?

explanation.correct: A legal/litigation hold formally requires preservation of potentially relevant data and suspends normal retention/deletion while litigation is anticipated or active.

distractors.A: Data minimization limits how much data is collected/kept — not a litigation preservation order.
distractors.B: Right to be forgotten is a privacy right to ERASE data — the opposite of preserving it.
distractors.D: Chain of custody documents evidence handling, not the organization-wide preservation order.

explanation.exam_pattern: Preserve data + suspend deletion for anticipated litigation = legal hold; then e-discovery produces it.

questions.stem: Running the annual security-awareness training and performing employee background checks are examples of which control CATEGORY?

explanation.correct: Operational controls are carried out primarily by PEOPLE as part of day-to-day operations — awareness training, background checks, and access reviews are operational.

distractors.A: Technical (logical) controls are implemented by technology (firewalls, encryption, MFA).
distractors.B: Managerial (administrative) controls are strategic — risk assessments, policies, and security planning — not the hands-on execution.
distractors.C: Physical controls are tangible barriers (locks, guards, fences, bollards).

explanation.exam_pattern: Category = who/what implements it: managerial (policy/risk planning), operational (people doing day-to-day), technical (tech enforces), physical (tangible barrier).

questions.stem: A motion-activated camera records and sends the SOC an alert the moment someone enters a restricted area after hours. Which control TYPE is the camera acting as here?

explanation.correct: Recording and alerting IDENTIFIES activity as it happens — a detective control. (The camera's visible presence can also deter, but the record-and-alert function is detection.)

distractors.A: Corrective controls act after an incident to restore/repair (e.g., restoring from backup).
distractors.B: Preventive controls STOP an event before it happens (a locked door, a firewall rule); the camera does not block entry.
distractors.C: Compensating controls are substitutes used when the primary control is not feasible.

explanation.exam_pattern: Type = what it DOES vs the event: preventive/deterrent (before), detective (identifies during/after), corrective (fixes after), compensating (stand-in), directive (instructs).

questions.stem: An e-commerce site uses redundant servers and load balancing so it stays reachable even if one server crashes during a sale. Which part of the CIA triad does this protect?

explanation.correct: Availability ensures authorized users can reach systems/data when needed; redundancy, load balancing, and failover are classic availability controls.

distractors.A: Confidentiality keeps data secret from unauthorized parties (encryption, access control).
distractors.C: Integrity ensures data is accurate and unaltered (hashing, digital signatures).
distractors.D: Non-repudiation proves who performed an action and is not part of the CIA triad.

explanation.exam_pattern: CIA: Confidentiality (secrecy), Integrity (unaltered), Availability (accessible). Redundancy/backup/failover/load balancing → availability.

questions.stem: A user types a username and then a password; the system confirms the password matches the stored credential for that account before any access is granted. Which step is the password check performing?

explanation.correct: Authentication is PROVING a claimed identity — verifying the password (something you know) matches the stored credential.

distractors.A: Identification is merely CLAIMING an identity (typing the username); it is not proof.
distractors.C: Accounting records what the authenticated user did (an audit trail).
distractors.D: Authorization happens AFTER authentication and decides what the user may access.

explanation.exam_pattern: Identify (claim) -> Authenticate (prove) -> Authorize (permit) -> Account (log). Verifying a credential = authentication.

questions.stem: In a Zero Trust architecture, a gateway sits in the traffic path to a protected resource and, acting on the decision relayed from the control plane, opens or drops each connection. Which component is this?

explanation.correct: The Policy Enforcement Point, in the DATA plane, allows, monitors, and terminates connections to the resource according to the control plane's decision.

distractors.A: The Policy Engine (control plane) MAKES the grant/deny decision; it does not sit in the traffic path.
distractors.B: The Policy Administrator (control plane) relays the decision and sets up/tears down the session, but the PEP is the enforcement gateway.
distractors.C: The Subject is the user/device requesting access, not an enforcement component.

explanation.exam_pattern: Control plane = Policy Engine (decides) + Policy Administrator (relays/sets up); data plane = Policy Enforcement Point (allows/blocks/monitors the actual connection).

questions.stem: A warehouse needs a motion sensor that covers a large open area and can detect movement even through thin, non-metallic partitions by emitting radio energy and measuring the reflection. Which sensor fits BEST?

explanation.correct: Microwave sensors emit radio waves and detect motion from changes in the reflected signal; they cover large areas and can sense through thin non-metal materials.

distractors.A: An ultrasonic sensor uses high-frequency SOUND waves and is typically shorter-range and more affected by obstacles.
distractors.B: A pressure sensor triggers on weight/force applied to a surface (e.g., a floor mat), not open-area motion.
distractors.C: A passive infrared (PIR) sensor detects a moving body's HEAT within line of sight and cannot see through walls.

explanation.exam_pattern: Sensors: infrared (body heat, line of sight), microwave (radio reflection, large area/thin walls), ultrasonic (sound), pressure (weight/force).

questions.stem: A core-switch upgrade is scheduled for 2:00 a.m. Sunday, the period of lowest business activity, so any disruption affects the fewest users. What is this pre-approved period called?

explanation.correct: A maintenance window is a scheduled, approved time — usually during low activity — for performing changes so impact is minimized.

distractors.B: A change freeze is a period during which NO changes are allowed (e.g., end-of-quarter).
distractors.C: A backout (rollback) plan is the documented way to UNDO the change if it fails, not the time it runs.
distractors.D: An SLA defines service commitments between parties, not a change's scheduled time.

explanation.exam_pattern: Change-management terms: maintenance window (when), backout plan (how to undo), impact analysis (what could break), approval/CAB (who signs off).

questions.stem: An enterprise needs a dedicated, tamper-resistant appliance to GENERATE, store, and manage cryptographic keys for many servers and to offload bulk encryption operations. Which solution is designed for this?

explanation.correct: An HSM is a dedicated, tamper-resistant device (appliance or card) for enterprise-scale key generation, storage, management, and crypto acceleration across many systems.

distractors.A: A TPM is a chip bound to a SINGLE host (e.g., for that machine's disk-encryption keys), not a multi-server enterprise key manager.
distractors.B: A CSR is a request sent to a CA to obtain a certificate, not a key-management device.
distractors.D: A KDC issues tickets in Kerberos authentication; it is not a key-storage appliance.

explanation.exam_pattern: TPM = per-device chip (one machine's keys); HSM = enterprise, tamper-resistant key manager/accelerator for many systems.

questions.stem: To slow down offline brute-force cracking of stored password hashes, developers run each password through a deliberately slow, repeated hashing function such as bcrypt, PBKDF2, or Argon2. What is this technique called?

explanation.correct: Key stretching repeatedly hashes (and salts) a low-entropy secret with a purposely expensive function so each guess costs an attacker far more time — bcrypt/PBKDF2/Argon2 are built for it.

distractors.B: Key escrow stores a copy of keys with a third party for recovery.
distractors.C: Salting adds a unique random value so identical passwords hash differently and defeats precomputed (rainbow-table) attacks; it is often combined with stretching but does not add CPU cost per guess.
distractors.D: Steganography hides data inside other media (images, audio).

explanation.exam_pattern: Salt (unique value -> stops precomputation) + key stretching (slow, repeated hashing -> raises per-guess cost). bcrypt/PBKDF2/Argon2 = key-stretching functions.

questions.stem: A company wants ONE certificate that secures its main domain and ANY current or future subdomain under it (shop.example.com, mail.example.com, vpn.example.com, ...) without reissuing. Which certificate type fits BEST?

explanation.correct: A wildcard certificate (CN/SAN of *.example.com) secures the domain and all first-level subdomains with a single cert, so new subdomains need no reissue.

distractors.A: A self-signed certificate is not issued by a trusted CA and browsers will not trust it by default.
distractors.B: A root CA certificate is the trust anchor used to sign other certificates, not to secure a website's subdomains.
distractors.C: A code-signing certificate signs software, not web hosts.

explanation.exam_pattern: Wildcard (*.domain) = all first-level subdomains, one cert. SAN cert = several specific, possibly DIFFERENT names/domains listed explicitly.

questions.stem: A certificate authority periodically publishes a digitally signed file listing the serial numbers of all certificates it has revoked before their expiration, which clients can download and cache. What is this mechanism?

explanation.correct: A CRL is a CA-signed, periodically published list of revoked certificate serial numbers; clients download it to check whether a certificate is still valid.

distractors.A: Key escrow stores keys for recovery; it has nothing to do with revocation status.
distractors.B: A CSR requests a new certificate from a CA.
distractors.C: OCSP checks the status of a SINGLE certificate in REAL TIME via a responder query, rather than downloading a whole list — lighter and more current than a CRL.

explanation.exam_pattern: Revocation: CRL (full signed list, periodically downloaded, can be stale) vs OCSP (real-time, single-cert query); OCSP stapling has the server present a time-stamped status.

questions.stem: Sales staff routinely connect their laptops to free, open (unencrypted) Wi-Fi at airports and cafes. An attacker on the same network captures their unencrypted traffic. Which THREAT VECTOR does this exploit?

explanation.correct: Connecting over an open, unencrypted wireless network is an unsecure-network vector — nearby attackers can eavesdrop or run on-path attacks. Mitigate with a VPN and TLS everywhere.

distractors.A: A supply-chain vector is abuse via a trusted vendor/MSP or a tampered component, not public Wi-Fi.
distractors.B: Removable media is a USB/external-drive vector.
distractors.C: Default credentials is leaving vendor-set logins (e.g., admin/admin) in place.

explanation.exam_pattern: Threat VECTOR = the path in. Open/rogue Wi-Fi = unsecure network -> VPN + TLS; USB drop = removable media; vendor compromise = supply chain.

questions.stem: An attacker crafts a highly tailored email aimed specifically at a company's CFO, referencing a genuine pending acquisition, to trick that executive into authorizing a wire transfer. Which social-engineering attack is this?

explanation.correct: Whaling is spear phishing aimed at a HIGH-VALUE executive ('big fish') such as a CEO or CFO, using tailored, credible details to exploit their authority.

distractors.A: Smishing is phishing delivered by SMS text message.
distractors.B: Shoulder surfing is observing someone's screen/keypad to steal information.
distractors.D: A watering-hole attack compromises a website the target group is known to visit.

explanation.exam_pattern: Phishing (broad) -> spear phishing (targeted) -> whaling (targeted at a senior executive). Channel variants: vishing (voice), smishing (SMS).

questions.stem: A disgruntled administrator inserts hidden code into a production server that will delete all payroll records automatically IF his own user account is ever disabled. Which type of malicious code is this?

explanation.correct: A logic bomb is dormant code that triggers a malicious payload when a specific CONDITION or time is met — here, the admin's account being disabled.

distractors.A: Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment.
distractors.C: A worm self-propagates across hosts over a network; it is not a conditional trigger.
distractors.D: A rootkit hides at a privileged level to maintain stealthy access.

explanation.exam_pattern: Condition/time trigger = logic bomb; self-spread = worm; encrypt+extort = ransomware; hide/privilege = rootkit; disguised installer = trojan.

questions.stem: In an airport, an attacker stands up a rogue Wi-Fi access point broadcasting the SAME SSID as the legitimate airport network, so victims associate to it and the attacker intercepts their traffic. Which attack is this?

explanation.correct: An evil twin is a rogue access point impersonating a legitimate SSID to lure clients into connecting, enabling eavesdropping and on-path attacks. WPA3, validating networks, and VPN use mitigate it.

distractors.A: A SYN flood is a denial-of-service that exhausts half-open TCP connections.
distractors.C: DNS cache poisoning injects false records into a resolver's cache.
distractors.D: ARP poisoning forges ARP replies on a local LAN to redirect traffic — not a rogue wireless AP.

explanation.exam_pattern: Rogue AP with a spoofed/duplicate SSID = evil twin (wireless on-path). LAN redirect via forged ARP = ARP poisoning.

questions.stem: A web form passes a user-supplied value straight into an operating-system shell command. An attacker enters '; cat /etc/passwd' and the server runs it, returning the file. Which attack is this?

explanation.correct: OS command injection occurs when unsanitized input is passed to a system shell, letting the attacker run arbitrary OS commands. Fix with strict input validation/allow-listing and safe APIs (avoid shell calls).

distractors.B: SQL injection targets a DATABASE query (e.g., ' OR '1'='1), not the OS shell.
distractors.C: XSS injects script that runs in other users' BROWSERS.
distractors.D: CSRF tricks an authenticated user's browser into submitting an unwanted request; it does not run server-side OS commands.

explanation.exam_pattern: Input reaches a shell = command injection; a SQL query = SQLi; a victim's browser = XSS. Defense for all: validate/encode input, least privilege.

questions.stem: A review finds a public web server deployed with directory listing enabled, verbose error messages exposed, and the vendor's default admin account still active. Which category of vulnerability do these findings represent?

explanation.correct: These are classic misconfigurations — insecure defaults and sloppy hardening that expose the system. Remediate with secure baselines/hardening and by disabling defaults.

distractors.B: A buffer overflow overwrites memory via oversized input to a fixed buffer.
distractors.C: A zero-day is an unknown flaw with no patch available — these issues are known, avoidable settings.
distractors.D: A race condition (e.g., TOCTOU) exploits timing between a check and a use.

explanation.exam_pattern: Default creds + unneeded features + exposed errors = misconfiguration -> apply a secure baseline/hardening checklist.

questions.stem: A company wants to limit the damage if a single user's password is phished. Which TWO mitigations MOST directly reduce the impact of one compromised credential? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: MFA means a stolen password alone is not enough to log in (the attacker still lacks the second factor), and least privilege limits what any one compromised account can reach or do.

distractors.A: Increasing the maximum password AGE lets passwords live LONGER before rotation, which does not reduce the impact of a compromise.
distractors.B: Disabling the host firewall removes a protection and widens exposure.

explanation.exam_pattern: Contain a single-credential compromise with MFA (blocks reuse) + least privilege (limits blast radius). Segmentation and monitoring help too.

questions.stem: A data-center network uses a central controller that computes forwarding decisions and pushes them to switches through APIs, separating the control plane from the data plane. Which architecture model is this?

explanation.correct: SDN decouples the control plane (a centralized controller making forwarding decisions) from the data plane (switches forwarding traffic), programmed via APIs for agility and central policy.

distractors.A: Serverless runs event-driven functions without managing servers — a compute model, not network control.
distractors.B: Microservices decompose an APPLICATION into small services.
distractors.C: IaC provisions infrastructure from version-controlled files; it can configure SDN but is not the control/data-plane split itself.

explanation.exam_pattern: SDN = centralized control plane + programmable data plane via APIs. Watch for 'controller' + 'separates control and data plane'.

questions.stem: A smart-building controller is a system-on-chip device running a stripped-down real-time OS with limited memory; it cannot host an EDR agent and is difficult to patch. Which characteristic MOST increases its security risk?

options.text: Limited compute and patchability of an embedded system

explanation.correct: Embedded/IoT devices (SoC, RTOS) have constrained compute, often cannot run endpoint protection, and are hard or slow to patch — so compensating controls (segmentation, network monitoring) are key.

distractors.B: A container packages an application to share a host OS kernel; it is not an embedded hardware device.
distractors.C: A serverless function is cloud event-driven code, not a physical SoC device.
distractors.D: A Type 1 hypervisor runs VMs on bare metal — not a resource-constrained embedded controller.

explanation.exam_pattern: Embedded/IoT/ICS = constrained, weak patch/monitoring story -> isolate on segmented networks + compensating controls.

questions.stem: A company wants central visibility and policy enforcement (DLP, access rules, threat protection) between its users and the MANY SaaS applications they use. Which solution sits between users and cloud services to provide this?

explanation.correct: A CASB sits between users and cloud/SaaS providers (inline or via API) to enforce visibility, access policy, DLP, and threat protection across cloud usage.

distractors.A: A host-based IDS monitors a single host's activity, not cloud-service usage broadly.
distractors.C: A jump server is a hardened pivot host for administering internal systems.
distractors.D: Local disk encryption protects data at rest on a device, not SaaS policy enforcement.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Policy/visibility between users and cloud/SaaS apps' = CASB. Often paired with SSO and DLP.

questions.stem: Under the shared responsibility model for a Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) application, which task remains the CUSTOMER's responsibility?

options.text: Securing the hypervisor and physical hosts
Managing user accounts, access, and data in the application

explanation.correct: With SaaS, the provider runs the app, OS, and infrastructure; the customer still owns their DATA, user identities/access, and in-app configuration (plus their own endpoints).

distractors.A: The hypervisor and physical data center are always the provider's responsibility.
distractors.B: The provider maintains the underlying OS in SaaS.
distractors.C: Patching the application is the SaaS provider's job.

explanation.exam_pattern: More 'as-a-service' = provider owns more. SaaS customer still owns data + identity/access + configuration; IaaS adds OS/app/runtime to the customer.

questions.stem: To protect a public web application specifically against layer-7 attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting, a team deploys a device that inspects HTTP/HTTPS requests and blocks malicious payloads. Which control is this?

explanation.correct: A WAF understands HTTP(S) and application-layer attacks (SQLi, XSS, etc.), filtering or blocking malicious requests to a web app — protection a generic firewall cannot provide.

distractors.A: A plain reverse proxy relays requests and may terminate TLS but, without inspection, does not block app-layer attacks.
distractors.B: A network IPS inspects broadly for signatures but is not specialized for a web app's HTTP logic like a WAF.
distractors.C: A stateful network firewall filters by IP/port/session at L3/L4 and does not parse application payloads for SQLi/XSS.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Protect a web app from SQLi/XSS at layer 7' = WAF. Generic firewall = L3/L4 ports; IPS = network signatures.

questions.stem: An inline security appliance is configured so that if it loses power or crashes, network traffic continues to pass THROUGH uninterrupted. Which design is this, and its trade-off?

explanation.correct: Fail-open means a failure lets traffic keep flowing — prioritizing AVAILABILITY, at the cost of security during the outage (traffic is uninspected/unfiltered).

distractors.A: Fail-closed (fail-secure) BLOCKS traffic on failure — prioritizing security over availability; the opposite of what is described.
distractors.B: An air gap physically isolates a network; it is not a failure mode.
distractors.D: Clustering adds redundant nodes for fault tolerance; it is not the behavior of a single device on failure.

explanation.exam_pattern: Fail-open = keep flowing (availability first); fail-closed/fail-secure = block (security first). Choose per the asset's priority.

questions.stem: Remote employees use an encrypted VPN to reach internal systems. Security wants ALL of their internet-bound traffic to also pass through the corporate gateway for inspection, not just traffic destined for internal resources. Which VPN configuration achieves this?

explanation.correct: A full-tunnel VPN routes ALL client traffic (including internet-bound) through the corporate gateway, so everything can be inspected and policy-enforced — at the cost of more bandwidth/latency.

distractors.A: A clientless reverse proxy brokers specific web apps, not all of a client's traffic.
distractors.C: A split tunnel sends only corporate-bound traffic through the VPN while internet traffic goes directly out — the opposite of the requirement.
distractors.D: A site-to-site IPsec tunnel connects two networks/offices, not a roaming remote user's full traffic.

explanation.exam_pattern: Full tunnel = all traffic via gateway (max inspection). Split tunnel = only corp traffic via VPN (better performance, less visibility).

questions.stem: A security architect must protect sensitive data AT REST on servers and laptops. Which TWO technologies directly protect data at rest? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: Full-disk encryption protects everything stored on a drive, and database/column-level encryption protects specific stored fields — both secure data AT REST.

distractors.B: An IPsec VPN also protects data IN TRANSIT between endpoints, not at rest.
distractors.D: TLS protects data IN TRANSIT across a network (HTTPS), not data sitting on disk.

explanation.exam_pattern: At rest = FDE, file/database/record-level encryption. In transit = TLS, IPsec/VPN. In use = secure enclave/memory encryption.

questions.stem: A hospital wants to release a dataset for public research. It PERMANENTLY strips and aggregates all direct and indirect identifiers so that no record can ever be traced back to an individual — with no key kept to reverse it. Which technique is this?

explanation.correct: Anonymization irreversibly removes/aggregates identifiers so individuals cannot be re-identified; because there is no reversing key, truly anonymized data falls outside most privacy-law scope.

distractors.A: Pseudonymization replaces identifiers with REVERSIBLE pseudonyms (a separate key can re-identify), so it is not irreversible.
distractors.B: Tokenization swaps a value for a token with the mapping held in a vault — reversible by design.
distractors.D: Data masking hides parts of a value for display (e.g., ****-4417) but the underlying data still exists.

explanation.exam_pattern: Irreversible, no key = anonymization. Reversible with a key/vault = pseudonymization/tokenization. Display-only hiding = masking.

questions.stem: A full backup runs every Sunday. Each weeknight's job backs up everything changed SINCE SUNDAY'S full backup and does NOT clear the archive bit, so each nightly backup grows larger through the week. Which backup type is in use?

explanation.correct: A differential backup copies all data changed since the last FULL backup and leaves the archive bit set, so it grows each day; restore needs only the full + the latest differential.

distractors.A: An incremental backup copies data changed since the last backup of ANY type and clears the archive bit, so each is small; restore needs the full + every incremental in order.
distractors.B: A full backup copies everything every time.
distractors.D: A snapshot is a point-in-time image (often of a VM/volume), not this rotating file-backup scheme.

explanation.exam_pattern: Differential = since last FULL (grows, archive bit kept; restore = full + last diff). Incremental = since last ANY (small, archive bit cleared; restore = full + all increments).

questions.stem: To minimize disaster-recovery cost, a company leases a backup facility that has space, power, and network drops but NO installed servers and NO current data; bringing it online would take days. Which recovery site type is this?

explanation.correct: A cold site provides only the basic facility (space/power/connectivity) with no ready hardware or data — cheapest to maintain but the slowest to recover (days).

distractors.A: A failover cluster is same-site/near-real-time redundancy, not an alternate DR facility class.
distractors.B: A hot site is fully equipped with hardware AND near-real-time data, ready almost immediately (most expensive).
distractors.C: A warm site has some hardware/connectivity but not current data, recovering in hours.

explanation.exam_pattern: Cold (empty shell, cheap, days) < Warm (some kit, hours) < Hot (ready + data, minutes, costly). Cost and speed rise together.

questions.stem: A security team argues that before any other control can be effective, the organization must first build and continuously maintain a complete, accurate record of every hardware device and software package it owns. Which asset-management practice is this?

explanation.correct: An accurate, current asset inventory (enumeration) is foundational — you cannot patch, monitor, or protect what you do not know you have.

distractors.A: Data classification labels data by sensitivity — important, but not an inventory of hardware/software.
distractors.B: A penetration test assesses exploitability; it presumes you already know your assets.
distractors.C: A change log records modifications over time, not a complete catalog of owned assets.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Can't protect what you can't see' -> asset inventory/enumeration first. Feeds vulnerability management, monitoring, and licensing.

questions.stem: When HR marks a new hire active, a workflow automatically creates the user's accounts, assigns group memberships based on job role, and emails setup instructions — and on termination it automatically disables everything. Which automation use case does this BEST illustrate?

explanation.correct: Orchestrating account creation, role-based access, and timely deprovisioning is the user provisioning/deprovisioning use case — it enforces consistency and ensures access is revoked promptly on offboarding.

distractors.A: Vulnerability scanning finds flaws in systems; it is not account management.
distractors.B: Security regression testing re-tests code for reintroduced flaws.
distractors.C: CI/CD automates building, testing, and deploying SOFTWARE, not the user-account lifecycle.

explanation.exam_pattern: Automation use cases: user/account provisioning + deprovisioning (consistency, fast offboarding), guard rails, ticket enrichment, resource provisioning, baseline enforcement.

questions.stem: After eliminating the malware and closing the exploited vulnerability, the team rebuilds the affected server from a known-good image, restores its data, validates it, and returns it to production under heightened monitoring. Which incident-response phase is this?

explanation.correct: Recovery restores systems to normal operation — rebuild/restore, validate, and monitor closely before and after return to service — following eradication.

distractors.A: Eradication is REMOVING the threat and root cause (the malware and the vulnerability) — already completed here.
distractors.B: Lessons learned is the post-incident review conducted after recovery.
distractors.C: Containment limits spread (e.g., isolating the host) and comes before eradication.

explanation.exam_pattern: IR order: Preparation -> Detection/Analysis -> Containment -> Eradication -> Recovery -> Lessons Learned. Rebuild/restore/validate/monitor = recovery.

questions.stem: Responders arrive at a powered-ON, compromised workstation. Following the order of volatility, which TWO types of VOLATILE evidence should be captured BEFORE the machine is shut down? (Choose two.)

options.text: Active network connections and running processes

explanation.correct: RAM contents and live state (network connections, running processes, ARP/routing tables) are VOLATILE and lost at power-off, so they are collected first with proper tools.

distractors.A: Tape backups are among the LEAST volatile and are collected last (or already archived).
distractors.D: Files on the hard drive are non-volatile and persist across a reboot, so they are imaged after volatile data.

explanation.exam_pattern: Order of volatility (most->least): CPU cache/registers -> RAM -> network/process state -> disk -> remote logs -> backups/archives. Capture live memory/connections before shutdown.

questions.stem: In a hospital system, permissions are bundled into job functions — 'Nurse', 'Physician', 'Billing Clerk' — and each user simply inherits the permissions of the role they are assigned. Which access-control MODEL is this?

explanation.correct: RBAC grants permissions to ROLES that map to job functions; users get access by their role assignment, which simplifies administration and enforces least privilege consistently.

distractors.A: ABAC decides access dynamically from ATTRIBUTES/policies (user dept, device, time, location), not a fixed role.
distractors.C: MAC enforces access via system-set security LABELS/clearances (e.g., Confidential/Secret) that users cannot change.
distractors.D: DAC lets the data OWNER grant access at their discretion (e.g., file permissions).

explanation.exam_pattern: RBAC = by job role; DAC = owner's discretion; MAC = labels/clearance (most rigid); ABAC = attribute/policy-driven (most granular).

questions.stem: Network devices are configured to immediately send an unsolicited alert to the management server the instant an interface goes down, instead of waiting to be polled. Which mechanism is this?

explanation.correct: An SNMP trap is an unsolicited, event-driven notification sent by an agent to the SNMP manager when a defined condition (like a link failure) occurs — no poll required.

distractors.A: SNMP polling (GET) is the manager REQUESTING values on an interval — the device waits to be asked, which the scenario rules out.
distractors.C: Syslog also forwards event messages, but the described SNMP agent-to-manager event notification driven by poll-vs-push is specifically a trap.
distractors.D: NetFlow exports traffic-FLOW statistics (who talked to whom), not device event alerts.

explanation.exam_pattern: SNMP trap = device pushes an event alert (unsolicited). SNMP GET/poll = manager pulls values. NetFlow = flow stats. Syslog = log messages.

questions.stem: A tester runs an automated tool that sends crafted and malicious inputs to a RUNNING web application from the outside — with no access to the source code — to uncover flaws such as injection and authentication bypass. Which testing technique is this?

explanation.correct: DAST tests a running application from the outside (black-box), observing how it responds to malicious input — good at finding runtime, injection, and auth flaws without source code.

distractors.A: A credentialed vulnerability scan logs into hosts to check patch/config levels; it is not application-logic input testing of a running app.
distractors.C: SCA inventories third-party/open-source COMPONENTS and their known CVEs, not live input testing.
distractors.D: SAST analyzes SOURCE CODE (or binaries) BEFORE execution — the opposite approach.

explanation.exam_pattern: SAST = source, pre-run (white-box). DAST = running app, outside-in (black-box). SCA = dependency/known-CVE analysis.

questions.stem: A business manager OWNS a customer dataset and sets its classification and handling rules. The database administration team then implements the backups, access permissions, and encryption that enforce those rules day to day. What is the DBA team's governance ROLE?

explanation.correct: A data custodian/steward is responsible for the day-to-day technical protection of data — backups, access enforcement, encryption — per the owner's requirements.

distractors.A: A data controller (privacy-law term) determines the purposes and means of processing personal data.
distractors.C: The data owner (the business manager here) is accountable for the data and sets its classification and rules — not the hands-on implementer.
distractors.D: A data subject is the individual the personal data is about.

explanation.exam_pattern: Owner = accountable, sets classification; Custodian/steward = implements/maintains protection; Controller = decides processing (GDPR); Processor = processes on the controller's behalf.

questions.stem: A document lists the exact, numbered steps a help-desk technician must follow to disable accounts, collect assets, and revoke access when an employee is terminated. Which governance document TYPE is this?

explanation.correct: A procedure is a detailed, step-by-step set of instructions for performing a specific task — here, the offboarding steps.

distractors.B: A guideline is a non-mandatory recommendation.
distractors.C: A standard specifies mandatory specifics (e.g., required tools or settings), narrower than a policy but not a step list.
distractors.D: A policy is the high-level, mandatory statement of intent ('accounts must be revoked promptly on termination'), not the steps.

explanation.exam_pattern: Policy (what/why, mandatory) -> Standard (specific requirements) -> Procedure (how, exact steps) -> Guideline (recommended best practice).

questions.stem: After a company applies all the controls it has chosen, some risk still remains. The leftover risk that management reviews and chooses to live with is BEST described as?

explanation.correct: Residual risk is the risk that REMAINS after controls are applied; management must evaluate and formally accept it (or add further treatment).

distractors.A: Transferred risk is risk shifted to a third party (e.g., insurance), a treatment choice rather than the remaining risk.
distractors.C: Risk appetite is the amount/type of risk an organization is WILLING to pursue — a threshold, not the leftover amount.
distractors.D: Inherent risk is the risk BEFORE any controls are applied.

explanation.exam_pattern: Inherent (before controls) -> apply controls -> Residual (after controls); accept residual only if within risk appetite/tolerance.

questions.stem: Under an existing master agreement with a consultancy, the two parties sign a document that lists the EXACT deliverables, milestones, timeline, and acceptance criteria for one specific security-assessment engagement. Which document is this?

explanation.correct: An SOW defines the specific work for a given project — deliverables, milestones, schedule, acceptance criteria — typically executed under an overarching MSA.

distractors.A: An MOU is a non-binding statement of intent between parties.
distractors.B: An SLA defines measurable service metrics (uptime/response) and penalties.
distractors.D: The MSA is the overarching contract setting general legal/business terms that each SOW falls under — not the per-project specifics.

explanation.exam_pattern: MSA = master terms (once) -> SOW = specific project work/deliverables (per engagement). SLA = service metrics. MOU = intent.

questions.stem: Two partner agencies sign a NON-BINDING document expressing their shared intentions and broad expectations to cooperate on a project, with no enforceable obligations, metrics, or penalties. Which document is this?

explanation.correct: An MOU (or MOA) is a generally non-binding document stating the parties' shared intent and expectations to work together, without the enforceable specifics of a contract.

distractors.A: An SLA is a binding, measurable commitment (uptime/response) with consequences for misses.
distractors.B: A BPA defines the terms of a business partnership (roles, responsibilities, profit sharing).
distractors.C: An NDA is a binding agreement protecting the confidentiality of shared information.

explanation.exam_pattern: MOU/MOA = intent, usually non-binding. SLA = measurable metrics + penalties. BPA = partnership terms. NDA = confidentiality.

questions.stem: Under GDPR, a retailer decides what customer personal data to collect and why, then hires a cloud email-marketing company that stores and processes that data STRICTLY on the retailer's documented instructions. Which role does the cloud company play?

explanation.correct: A data processor processes personal data ON BEHALF of, and under the instructions of, the controller — exactly the cloud email provider's role here.

distractors.A: 'Data owner' is an internal governance role, not the GDPR term for this relationship.
distractors.C: The data controller (the retailer) determines the PURPOSES and MEANS of processing.
distractors.D: A supervisory authority is the regulator that enforces GDPR, not a party processing the data.

explanation.exam_pattern: GDPR: Controller decides why/how (purposes/means); Processor acts on the controller's instructions. Both carry obligations.

questions.stem: A retailer that stores, processes, and transmits payment-card data must comply with a security standard created and enforced by the major card brands through contracts — NOT by a government statute. Which framework is this?

explanation.correct: PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) is a contractual, industry-mandated standard for organizations handling cardholder data; non-compliance brings fines or loss of card-processing privileges.

distractors.A: GDPR is an EU LAW protecting personal data/privacy.
distractors.C: HIPAA is a U.S. LAW protecting health information.
distractors.D: SOX is a U.S. LAW governing financial reporting and controls for public companies.

explanation.exam_pattern: PCI DSS = industry/contractual (cards). HIPAA (health), GDPR (EU privacy), SOX (financial reporting) = government laws/regulations.

questions.stem: A privacy policy states that the company will collect ONLY the personal data it genuinely needs for a stated purpose and will DELETE it once that purpose is fulfilled. Which TWO privacy principles are being applied? (Choose two.)

explanation.correct: Collecting only what is necessary is data minimization; deleting data once its purpose is met is storage/retention limitation — both core data-privacy principles (e.g., under GDPR).

distractors.C: Non-repudiation is a security property (proof of an action's origin), unrelated to these privacy principles.
distractors.D: Data sovereignty concerns the JURISDICTION/location where data is stored and whose laws apply, not how little is collected or how long it is kept.

explanation.exam_pattern: Privacy principles: minimization (collect the least needed), purpose limitation, storage/retention limitation (keep no longer than needed). Sovereignty = location/jurisdiction.

questions.stem: During an authorized penetration test, the tester directly interacts with the target — port-scanning its hosts and banner-grabbing running services to map the attack surface. Which reconnaissance type is this?

explanation.correct: Active reconnaissance directly probes the target (scanning, enumeration, banner grabbing), which is more informative but more detectable than passive methods.

distractors.B: Privilege escalation gains higher rights after access, not information gathering.
distractors.C: Passive reconnaissance gathers information WITHOUT touching the target (OSINT, public records, DNS/WHOIS) and is stealthier.
distractors.D: Pivoting is using a compromised host to reach other systems — a post-exploitation move, not recon.

explanation.exam_pattern: Passive recon = no direct contact (OSINT, stealthy). Active recon = direct probing (scans/enumeration, detectable). Both precede exploitation.

questions.stem: To give customers INDEPENDENT assurance over its controls, a SaaS provider hires an outside accounting firm to examine those controls and issue a formal attestation report (such as SOC 2). Which type of assessment is this?

explanation.correct: An external/third-party audit is performed by an independent outside party and yields an attestation (e.g., SOC 2) that customers and regulators can trust more than a self-review.

distractors.A: An internal audit is conducted by the organization's OWN staff for self-checking and readiness.
distractors.B: A self-assessment is the organization grading itself (lowest independence).
distractors.C: A tabletop exercise is a discussion-based incident-response drill, not a controls attestation.

explanation.exam_pattern: Independence ladder: self-assessment < internal audit < external/third-party audit/attestation (SOC 2, ISO certification) — more independence = more trust.

questions.stem: An organization requires employees to lock their screens and to store all sensitive documents and removable media in locked drawers whenever they step away from their workstation. Which security-awareness practice is this?

explanation.correct: A clean desk policy requires sensitive materials to be secured (and screens locked) when a workspace is unattended, reducing shoulder surfing, theft, and accidental exposure.

distractors.A: An acceptable use policy governs how employees may use company systems/resources, not desk tidiness.
distractors.B: Separation of duties splits critical tasks among people to prevent fraud — unrelated to an unattended desk.
distractors.C: Data classification labels data by sensitivity; it does not dictate securing a physical desk.

explanation.exam_pattern: 'Secure papers/media + lock screen when away' = clean desk policy (counters shoulder surfing and opportunistic data exposure).

questions.stem: A criminal syndicate runs a ransomware-as-a-service operation, renting its malware to affiliates and splitting the extortion profits. Which threat actor type and primary motivation does this describe?

explanation.correct: Profit-driven, structured criminal groups that run RaaS businesses to extort money are organized crime; their defining motivation is financial gain.

distractors.A: An unskilled attacker lacks the resources and organization to run a RaaS business.
